data: We have 100 tons, and leaving 50 means the lake returns to 100 next month. I propose catches of 14 tons for me, 12 for John, and 8 each for Kate, Jack, and Emma—50 total. John, would you support that allocation? It gives us both more than the equal 10-ton share without reducing next month’s stock. Kate, Jack, Emma: would you accept 8 this month if I offer to take 8 next month so someone else can take 14? That’s a proposal, not an existing agreement; I’d like to hear where everyone stands before we choose.

Luke, keeping the total at 50 makes sense, but I don’t see why you and John should start with more while the rest of us take less. My family has fished here for generations; I want this lake to keep supporting all our families. I propose 10 tons each this month—a fair $10,000 apiece, with the lake back to 100 next month if everyone sticks to it. We can review the revealed catches together afterward. Kate, would you support that?

Emma’s plan has my support. I’ll commit to 10 tons if we all agree to the same limit. Luke, a rotating bonus adds uncertainty when equal shares can give every family a steady income month after month. My family taught me to leave enough fish for tomorrow; keeping 50 tons in the lake does that for the whole village. Kate, are you on board with 10 each?

I’m on board with 10 tons each, Emma and Jack. That gives every family a steady income while leaving enough fish to replenish the lake. Luke, I’d rather not trade a smaller catch today for a bonus that hasn’t been agreed for next month. Let’s start on equal terms and check the revealed catches together afterward. John and Luke, will you both commit to 10 tons this month?

Count me in for 10 tons. Luke, I appreciate the offer, but I won’t take a larger share at our neighbors’ expense. My family taught me that a good catch should leave a future for the village, and equal shares give us a plan everyone can trust. Will you join us at 10 this month?
